title: Attention in Large Language Models Yields Efficient Zero-Shot Re-Rankers

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to enable accurate, efficient zero-shot document re-ranking with open-weight LLMs, avoiding autoregressive generation. Paper [8] ("RankVicuna") shares the same objective at the problem-class level: it aims to achieve zero-shot document re-ranking using open-source LLMs, explicitly addressing the inefficiencies and limitations of proprietary models. Paper [13] ("Scaling Down, LiTting Up") also targets efficient zero-shot listwise re-ranking, focusing on reducing computational costs and improving practicality, which aligns with the efficiency aspect of the contribution's purpose. Both papers substantively overlap with the stated objective.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, In-Context Re-ranking (ICR), aggregates attention weights from query tokens to document tokens across all layers/heads to compute token-level ranking scores, summing them per document. Paper [2] ("An Attention-Based Interactive Learning-to-Rank Model") employs attention-based mechanisms for ranking, focusing on token-level interactions between queries and documents, which is substantively equivalent to the primitive of using attention weights for ranking. Paper [21] ("Focused Attention Improves Document-Grounded Generation") also uses focused attention mechanisms to improve document-level tasks, which aligns with the underlying primitive of leveraging attention scores for document-level ranking. Both papers cover the mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design uses TREC and BEIR datasets for single-hop tasks and multi-hop tasks, measuring nDCG@10 and Recall@k. Paper [8] ("RankVicuna") evaluates zero-shot re-ranking using BEIR datasets and similar metrics (e.g., nDCG@10), which matches the benchmark family and metric semantics. Paper [13] ("Scaling Down, LiTting Up") also evaluates zero-shot listwise re-ranking using standard IR metrics like nDCG and Recall, applied to similar datasets. Both papers reuse the same evaluation design, covering this facet.

### Domain
The domain is information retrieval (IR) and LLM-based document re-ranking. Paper [8] ("RankVicuna") explicitly operates in the same domain, focusing on LLM-based document re-ranking for IR tasks. Paper [13] ("Scaling Down, LiTting Up") also works in the IR domain, targeting efficient zero-shot listwise re-ranking. Both papers address the same application area, covering the domain facet.

## Purpose

The purpose is to enable accurate, efficient zero-shot document re-ranking with open-weight LLMs without autoregressive generation (avoiding O(N) forward passes, ill-formed outputs, and reliance on proprietary models).

Paper [8] (RankVicuna) explicitly addresses "reranking in an information retrieval context" using open-source LLMs to avoid proprietary model dependence. Paper [1] investigates LLM-based re-ranking and notes "current state-of-the-art results heavily lean on the capabilities of the LLM being used" and proprietary models. Paper [13] addresses "efficient zero-shot listwise reranking" noting drawbacks of large LLMs. However, none of these specifically target the sub-objective of *avoiding autoregressive generation entirely* to enable use with weaker open-weight models via a non-generative mechanism. Paper [1] comes closest by addressing the proprietary model problem, but its solution is pre-filtering, not eliminating generation. The combination of "no autoregressive generation + O(1) forward passes + open-weight" as a unified purpose is not directly covered, but the high-level objective of "efficient zero-shot re-ranking with open-weight LLMs" is substantially covered by [8] and [13].

Paper [8] states the purpose of open-source LLM re-ranking, and [13] addresses efficiency of zero-shot listwise reranking. Together these cover the purpose at the problem-class level.

## Mechanism

The mechanism is: aggregate attention weights that document tokens receive from query tokens (across all layers/heads) as a relevance score, requiring only two forward passes. This is a cross-attention/self-attention aggregation approach for ranking.

Paper [2] uses attention-based learning-to-rank but in a supervised interactive setting, not zero-shot attention weight aggregation. Paper [20] uses co-attention for scoring. Paper [21] uses "focused attention" for document-grounded generation. Paper [11] ("Recall Aspects of Transformers for Text Ranking") is listed without abstract but its title suggests examining transformer attention for ranking. Paper [17] precomputes term representations for efficiency but uses standard scoring, not attention weight aggregation. None of these describe the specific primitive of aggregating query-to-document attention weights from a prompted LLM as a ranking signal with O(1) forward passes. The closest is [2] (attention-based ranking) but it's supervised LTR, not zero-shot attention weight extraction from a prompted LLM. No prior paper describes this specific primitive.

## Evaluation

The evaluation uses TREC + BEIR datasets with nDCG@10, re-ranking top-100 BM25, plus multi-hop tasks with Recall@k, and latency comparisons vs RankGPT.

Papers [8], [1], [13], [12], [7] all use BEIR/TREC benchmarks with nDCG@10 for zero-shot re-ranking evaluation. Paper [13] uses "competitive reranking effectiveness compared to recent state-of-the-art" on similar benchmarks. This evaluation design (BEIR/TREC, nDCG@10, re-rank BM25 top-100) is standard in the LLM re-ranking literature and clearly covered by [8], [12], [13].

## Domain

The domain is information retrieval / LLM re-ranking. Papers [1], [7], [8], [12], [13] all operate in exactly this domain.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to mitigate intrinsic biases in LLMs (e.g., position bias, attention toward titles/entities/punctuation) that corrupt attention-based ranking scores. Paper [6] explicitly addresses position bias in LLMs, particularly in the context of LLM-as-a-Judge, and introduces metrics to evaluate bias effects. Paper [1] discusses mitigating intrinsic biases in LLMs, including prompt brittleness caused by formatting and example selection, which aligns with the broader goal of addressing LLM biases. Paper [15] tackles position bias in ranking systems, though it focuses on streaming media services rather than LLMs. These papers share the same problem-class objective of mitigating intrinsic biases in ranking or decision systems.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves a calibration method using a content-free query ('N/A') to compute attention-aggregation scores, subtracting these from actual-query scores to isolate query-semantics-driven changes in attention. Paper [20] introduces calibration techniques to improve LLM performance in few-shot learning, addressing instability caused by biases in prompt formatting and example order, which overlaps conceptually with calibration for bias mitigation. Paper [25] systematically examines calibration methods for aligned LLMs, focusing on improving reliability and confidence calibration, which is conceptually similar to the proposed calibration mechanism. Paper [16] explores classifier calibration methods, but it focuses on binary classification rather than attention-based ranking. Paper [12] discusses calibration in optical systems, which is unrelated to LLMs or ranking tasks. No prior paper explicitly uses a content-free query ('N/A') for calibration in the described manner.

### Evaluation
The evaluation involves ablation studies on SciFact, FiQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultiHopQA datasets, measuring improvements in ranking scores and calibration overhead. Papers [9] and [10] evaluate LLM-based ranking methods using similar benchmark families (e.g., multi-hop QA datasets) and metrics for ranking effectiveness, which matches the evaluation design. Paper [6] evaluates position bias in LLMs using metrics like position consistency and preference fairness, which align with the evaluation design for bias mitigation. Paper [1] evaluates LLM bias mitigation but focuses on prompt brittleness rather than ranking scores. The evaluation design (benchmark family and metrics) is covered by prior work.

### Domain
The domain is LLM bias mitigation and re-ranking. Papers [9], [10], and [6] all operate in the domain of LLM-based ranking and bias mitigation, addressing intrinsic biases and re-ranking effectiveness. Paper [1] also addresses LLM bias mitigation but focuses on prompt brittleness rather than ranking. Paper [15] addresses position bias in ranking systems but focuses on streaming media services rather than LLMs. The domain is covered by prior work.

Still, [1] covers the same objective class: mitigate LLMs' intrinsic biases via internal attention manipulation. This is substantively equivalent at the problem-class level.

**MECHANISM: Content-free query ('N/A') calibration — compute attention scores with N/A query, subtract from actual-query scores to isolate query-semantics-driven attention; KV cache shared between passes.**

Paper [20] (Calibrate Before Use) uses a content-free input to estimate and subtract the model's prior bias: "we propose a simple calibration procedure that makes the model's prediction invariant to these factors... we estimate the model's bias by using a content-free input such as 'N/A'." This is essentially the same primitive: run the model with a content-free/null input, measure the baseline bias signal, subtract it from actual outputs. The application is different (few-shot classification vs. attention-based re-ranking), but the underlying mechanism — content-free query → measure intrinsic bias → subtract — is identical. The KV cache sharing is an efficiency detail, not a different primitive. This is clearly covered by [20].

The ablation design (component A vs. A+B) is standard. SciFact and FiQA are part of the BEIR benchmark family used widely. This evaluation design (standard IR benchmark + nDCG + component ablation) is covered by [3] and [9].

**DOMAIN: LLM bias mitigation / re-ranking.**

Papers [1], [3], [4], [5], [9], [10] all work in LLM-based re-ranking or LLM bias mitigation. This domain is clearly covered by multiple prior papers.
